R3.3.response:
This is the question we were least able to answer from the submitted evidence, and answering it properly changed what the paper claims.

The 60,606 flows per second reported in the submitted manuscript was an offline feature-extraction and inference rate. It was measured by reading feature vectors from a matrix and scoring them in a loop, with no control channel present, no OpenFlow messages, and no rule installation. It is not an ingest rate and it should not have been presented as one.

We therefore built a control plane and measured the controller rather than the model. The detector runs inside a controller process that exchanges genuine OpenFlow 1.3 messages with switch agents over TCP, with every encoding validated against the os-ken reference parser. At an offered rate of 3,000 packet-in events per second the controller saturates: it sustains 114 events per second end to end, including classification and rule installation, at 98.3 percent of one core and 176 MB resident, with a decision taking 6.61 ms at the median and 32.70 ms at the 99th percentile. Enabling attribution for every alert halves that to 61 events per second and nearly doubles the median decision to 11.33 ms.

Sweeping the offered rate locates the knee and shows what lies beyond it. The maximum is 77 events per second, reached at an offered rate of 500. Above that the goodput does not plateau, it collapses to roughly 35 events per second and stays there while the median round-trip time nearly triples. Offering more work returns less, which is queue behavior past saturation rather than the gradual degradation a throughput figure alone would suggest.

So the direct answer is that a single controller instance on this hardware cannot ingest 60,000 novel flows per second as individual table-miss events, and neither can it ingest 6,000. Reaching that order of magnitude requires that the flows not arrive as individual packet-in events at all. Switch-side aggregation, packet-in rate limiting and sampled export are the mechanisms, and Section VII-P quantifies what the first of them costs in flow-table occupancy. We also note a constraint that no aggregation policy removes: at the measured 386 bytes per packet-in, 60,000 events per second would require 23 MB/s on the control channel irrespective of controller CPU.

We have removed the throughput claim the question was asked about and replaced it with these measurements, including the ones that are unflattering.
R3.3.action: Built an OpenFlow 1.3 control plane with the detector inside the controller process, measured controller CPU, memory, decision latency, control-channel byte rate and the achieved ingest rate under fixed load, swept the offered rate to saturation and past it, and replaced the offline throughput claim with the measured ingest rate.
